checks.claim: Galileo timed bronze balls rolling down grooves cut in wooden ramps (a channel cut in a wooden moulding, a hard smooth bronze ball, timed by weighing water from a water clock)
checks.note: Two New Sciences, Third Day: 'a piece of wooden moulding or scantling' with a groove and 'a hard, smooth, and very round bronze ball', timed by water. Grokipedia Two_New_Sciences also: bronze balls, grooved tracks, a water clock.

checks.claim: He reasoned that a ball rolling down one ramp and up a second climbs almost back to its starting height, whatever the steepness of the second
checks.note: Grokipedia: a ball rolling down one incline and up another reaches 'the same elevation in the absence of friction or air resistance'; UVA (Fowler) gives the same, real balls falling a little short. 'Almost' is right for real balls.

checks.claim: KEY: with the second ramp laid flat and perfectly smooth, he concluded the ball would roll on forever at the same speed
checks.note: Two New Sciences, Fourth Day: a particle on a frictionless horizontal plane moves with 'a motion which is uniform and perpetual, provided the plane has no limits'. Grokipedia Two_New_Sciences: with the second plane horizontal the ball 'would continue in uniform rectilinear motion indefinitely'. Wikipedia Newton's laws: Galileo concluded the natural behaviour of a moving body was to keep moving. Nuance only (not an error at grade 7): historians note Galileo's 'horizontal' meant a surface concentric with the Earth (Wikipedia Inertia, 'circular inertia'); straight-line inertia came with Descartes and Newton. The question never says 'straight line', so it is safe.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (slows down with no slope to push it; stops at the flat; keeps speeding up) are not Galileo's conclusion and are false for a frictionless level plane
checks.note: TAU museum: on a smooth frictionless horizontal plane the body 'will neither accelerate nor decelerate'.

checks.claim: Context: real balls stop because of friction and the air; grass stops a ball sooner than smooth ice
Context: Aristotle taught that a pushed thing stops once nothing pushes it
checks.note: Grokipedia: violent motion needs a continuous applied force; 'the motion ceases immediately upon removal of the agent'. Wikipedia Inertia: on Earth moving things come to rest unless a force keeps moving them. (Aristotle had the air keep pushing a thrown body, but the simplified line stays true.)

checks.claim: Newton set out his first law, often called the law of inertia, in the Principia, 1687
checks.note: Grokipedia: first published in 1687 in the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica; the first law is 'often called the law of inertia'. OpenStax 4.2 agrees on the name.

checks.claim: KEY: a probe far from any star or planet, engines off, keeps moving straight on at the same speed
checks.note: NASA Glenn: a spacecraft 'will travel in a straight line if the forces on it are in balance'; a nearby planet's gravity or a rocket firing changes its path or speed.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (slows until it stops; stops at once; speeds up with no air) are false with no net force
checks.note: First law: constant speed in a straight line unless acted on by an unbalanced force.

checks.claim: Context: engines needed only to speed up, slow down or turn; on Earth friction and air stop moving things
In orbit a bathroom scale would read nothing for a floating object
checks.note: The scale falls with the object, so it gives no support force and reads zero; astronauts on the station measure mass with spring devices instead (space.com).

checks.claim: KEY: the steel toolbox is far harder to set moving than the pencil (mass, not weight, gives inertia)
checks.note: A satellite in orbit is 'weightless' yet 'still retains its mass and inertia'. A big steel toolbox is thousands of times the mass of a pencil, so 'far harder' is right and 'only by a little' is wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (equally easy since neither has weight; harder only by a little; the pencil harder) are false
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'greater mass implies stronger inertia'; inertia is directly proportional to mass.

checks.claim: Context: a NASA lesson has an astronaut struggling to push a one-ton satellite out of a space shuttle's cargo bay
checks.note: NASA Goddard: 'An astronaut in a space suit, in the space shuttle bay, tries to push a one-ton scientific satellite out of the bay, but the satellite proves very hard to move'; 'it has no weight, but it has one ton of mass'.

checks.claim: KEY: an unbuckled passenger lurches forward under hard braking because his body goes on moving as the car stops
checks.note: Grokipedia Inertia: when a car abruptly stops, passengers without seatbelts continue forward, an example of linear inertia.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (the braking car throws him forward; the seat behind pushes him; the air rushes forward with him) are false
checks.note: No forward force acts on him; the seat's friction on him points backward, if anything.

checks.claim: Context: unbuckled, he goes on until the dashboard or windshield stops him
checks.note: Grokipedia Seat_belt: 'the unrestrained torso pitched forward violently'; 'head impacts with dashboards or windshields'.

checks.claim: Context: a seat belt gives the slowing force, spread across the strong bones of the hips and shoulder
checks.note: Grokipedia: the belt 'distributes deceleration forces across the stronger bony structures of the pelvis and shoulder' (the three-point belt loads pelvis, rib cage and clavicle). 'Hips' for pelvis is a fair grade-7 word.

checks.claim: KEY: on a left bend the box slides to the right because it goes on straight while the car turns
checks.note: OpenStax 6.2: the feeling of sliding or being flung away from the centre of the turn happens 'because your body wants to continue moving in a straight line (as per Newton's first law)'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'An outward force flings it away from the bend' is false (no real outward force)
checks.note: Grokipedia: in an inertial frame 'no such outward force exists'; centrifugal force is fictitious, a bookkeeping tool only inside a rotating frame. OpenStax: 'This isn't an actual force that is acting on you'. Not defensible at grade 7, and the context says so plainly.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (weight pulls it to the outside; the turning car pushes it toward the door) are false
checks.note: Weight acts straight down; the car (seat friction, then the door) pushes the box inward, toward the centre of the bend, not outward.

checks.claim: Context: the seat's grip (friction) is too weak to turn the box with the car; the door swings round to meet it; the outward force passengers feel is not a real push
checks.note: OpenStax: friction supplies the centripetal force; without enough of it a body slides off 'in a straight line'; centrifugal force is 'not a real force but the result of an accelerating reference frame'.

checks.claim: KEY: the quick yank leaves the dishes, because friction has little time to act
checks.note: UCSB: 'friction cannot provide sufficient force to accelerate the objects appreciably during the short time' it takes to pull the cloth away; the trick 'arises from the inertia of the objects'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The slow tug, as it drags on the dishes less' is false
checks.note: Wisconsin Wonders of Physics: pulled slowly, friction 'will cause the tablecloth to pull the beaker with it'; UCSB: a slow pull drags everything along.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'Either one, as inertia holds the dishes still' and 'Neither, as the cloth always drags the dishes' are false
checks.note: Only the fast pull works; inertia is a resistance to change in motion, not a grip (OpenStax 4.2).

checks.claim: Context: friction acts either way; a slow tug gives it time to drag the dishes off; inertia is not a grip but resistance to a change in motion
checks.note: Wisconsin adds that friction is weaker in a fast pull (kinetic rather than static friction); the context's 'little time' account matches UCSB and stays true.

checks.claim: KEY: when the string snaps, the ball (seen from above) flies off in a straight line the way it was heading, along the edge of the circle (a tangent)
checks.note: Inertia carries it on in a straight line tangent to the circle; the string's tension was the only inward force (Grokipedia Centripetal_force: the tension supplies the inward force; with no inward force the body keeps the straight-line motion of the first law). 'Seen from directly above' rightly sets aside the ball's fall under gravity.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (keeps curving; straight out away from her, i.e. radially; a widening spiral) are false
checks.note: Michigan Tech demo: the velocity of a body in uniform circular motion is tangent to the circle, so on release it leaves along the tangent, not radially outward.

checks.claim: Context: in studies in the 1980s many college students expected a ball let go from a curved path to keep curving, an idea much like the old theory of impetus
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Studies conducted in the 1980s by Michael McCloskey and colleagues' found adults expecting curved paths for 'a ball released from a curved tube', a naive impetus view 'reminiscent of medieval physics', held by 'over 50% of college students'. McCloskey, Caramazza and Green, Science 210 (1980) 1139-1141, tested college students. A later summary gives about 30% for the ball-and-string problem itself; the context speaks of a ball let go from a curved path in general, so it stays true. It says 'much like' impetus, a resemblance the authors themselves drew, and does not claim the students held a full theory (later work, e.g. Psychonomic Society papers, questioned that).

checks.claim: KEY: a ball tossed straight up on a train moving steadily on a straight level track comes back down into his hand
checks.note: Illinois Ask the Van: the ball keeps the train's forward velocity, 'All motion is relative', 'No push is needed to maintain motion'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (a little behind; a little ahead; behind as far as the train has gone) are false for steady straight-line motion
checks.note: Only braking, speeding up or a curve would shift the landing point; the stem rules these out.

checks.claim: Context: Galileo argued the same in his Dialogue of 1632
checks.note: Printed in Florence by Landini in February 1632; the ship's mast argument is in it (Wikipedia Galileo's_ship). 'Argued' is right: Galileo discussed it without claiming to have done it.

checks.claim: Context: the object dropped from the top of the smoothly sailing ship's mast was 'a cannonball'
checks.note: Sources disagree. Grokipedia and Wikipedia (Galileo's_ship) say 'a cannonball dropped from the top of the mast'; but Tel Aviv University's Galileo museum describes the Dialogue's object as a stone that 'would fall to the base of the sailing ship's mast', and a Columbia lecture slide quoting the Dialogue has 'A stone dropped in the ship will fall at the same point'; Galileo's 1624 reply to Ingoli speaks of a rock. Safe fix: 'about a stone dropped from the top of a smoothly sailing ship's mast: it falls at the foot of the mast, not behind it.' The landing point (foot of the mast) is right in every source.

checks.claim: KEY: holding the hammer upright and striking the handle's end on the floor, the handle stops but the head keeps going, sliding farther down the handle
checks.note: UMD demonstration 'Inertia: Hammerhead': held upright with the handle struck sharply on the table, 'the head can be seen to move downwards along the handle', 'resisting the abrupt deceleration'.

checks.claim: This tightens a loose head (rather than pounding the head itself)
checks.note: University of Iowa: 'you don't tighten a hammer head by hitting it onto the handle' but by slamming the other end of the handle onto the table (inertia of mass); pounding the head 'will actually move off the handle'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (the floor's jolt drives the head down; gravity pulls harder at the jolt; the heavy head falls faster) are false
checks.note: The floor pushes up, only on the handle; gravity does not change at the jolt; heavy and light bodies fall with the same acceleration when air resistance is small (Grokipedia Galileo: 'no significant difference in acceleration between heavier and lighter objects').

checks.claim: Context: only the wood's friction acts to stop the head, so it slides farther on
checks.note: UMD notes the loose head has frictional resistance on the handle and moves on down it.

checks.claim: Stem: 'Johannes Kepler coined the word inertia from a Latin word meaning idle or sluggish'
checks.note: Kepler did not coin the word: inertia was already a Latin noun (from iners, unskilled, inactive) meaning unskilfulness and, by extension, 'inactivity, idleness, laziness' (Wiktionary, citing Lewis and Short). Kepler, writing in Latin, was the first to give it a sense close to the physics one, in the Epitome Astronomiae Copernicanae (1617-1621). Grokipedia Inertia: the term 'was first applied to physics by Johannes Kepler'; Wikipedia Inertia: 'first introduced by Johannes Kepler' and 'derived from the Latin word for idleness or laziness'. Fix: 'Johannes Kepler first used the Latin word inertia, meaning idleness or sluggishness, for a property of matter.' (or: 'brought the Latin word inertia, idleness, into physics').

checks.claim: Iners / inertia meaning idle or sluggish
checks.note: Grokipedia: iners, 'inactive', 'idle', 'sluggish'; Wikipedia: 'iners, meaning idle or sluggish'.

checks.claim: Newton later built his first law of motion on the idea
checks.note: OpenStax: Newton incorporated the concept of inertia into his first law, often called the law of inertia.

checks.claim: KEY: in Newton's physics inertia resists any change in the body's motion
checks.note: Grokipedia: inertia is the resistance of matter to changes in its state of motion, quantified by mass; Newton's vis insita, a power of resisting by which a body continues in its state of rest or uniform straight motion.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (makes a moving body slow down and stop; pushes a moving body to keep it going; pulls it toward the ground) are false in Newton's physics
checks.note: Slowing to rest is Kepler's older sense (rest as natural), not Newton's; inertia is not a force that pushes (Newton's vis inertiae acts only against a change of state); the pull toward the ground is gravity.

checks.claim: Context: Kepler took rest to be natural and meant only a resistance to being moved; for Newton inertia also keeps a moving body moving; more mass, more inertia
checks.note: Wikipedia: Kepler 'defined inertia only in terms of resistance to movement', presuming rest a natural state; Galileo and Newton unified rest and motion in one principle. Grokipedia: 'greater mass implies stronger inertia'.

unit_notes: One error: Q10 (90144df1cc) says Kepler 'coined the word inertia'; the Latin noun inertia (idleness) already existed, and Kepler first used it in physics. One uncertain: Q8 (c267604dd1) context calls the object dropped from Galileo's ship's mast a cannonball; Grokipedia and Wikipedia say cannonball, but Tel Aviv University's Galileo museum and a slide quoting the Dialogue say a stone; changing to 'a stone' is safe. Q1's Galileo ramps are told as Galileo argued them (Grokipedia Two_New_Sciences; the Fourth Day's 'uniform and perpetual, provided the plane has no limits'); historians' caveat that his 'horizontal' was a surface round the Earth does not touch the question, which says nothing of a straight line.
